sweep_summary: Two title-hits, both already in our bibliography. (1) Rhyasen Erdman 1997 'Stress in Stoney' (U Calgary MA, open at the Glottolog collectionscanada URL, 4,869,831 bytes, identical to the copy held since 9/13) was read for this sweep and copied into the working files: penultimate primary stress in verbs in both Alexis and Morley Stoney; Alexis nouns final; final stress on long vowels, monosyllabic roots and the perfective; alternating right-to-left secondary stress in Alexis vs second-syllable secondary in Morley; and an explicit rebuttal of Shaw's superheavy-VCC weight rule as lexical stress on the perfective morpheme. It refines the catalog's weight-hedged, right-edge coding (dialect split; 'weight' = vowel length in Alexis, disputed CVCC in Morley) but does not replace Shaw 1985a as the deciding source, since Shaw is the primary for Morley and RE's own rule statements rest on Alexis. (2) Shaw 1985a IJAL 51:1-18 (DOI 10.1086/465857) remains unread first-hand: uchicago 403 (pdf and landing), JSTOR challenge page, archive.org/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/UBC/core.ac.uk yield no open copy; the catalog's quotation is still carried via StressTyp2 passage 859 and Hayes 1995:267 n.19 (both re-read in held files). Shaw 1985b (Phonology Yearbook 2:173-202, DOI 10.1017/S0952675700000427) landing page reached: paywalled, extract has no Stoney stress sentence. Priority to acquire: Shaw 1985a high (Harvard online access listed).

new_statements.quote: p.56: 'Shaw (1985a) discloses an innovative stress pattern in Stoney that has no semblance to the other reported Dakota languages; primary stress is realized on the penultimate syllable. Another innovation found in Stoney, that is not found in Dakota, is secondary stress. Both Alexis Stoney and Morley Stoney share the innovative penultimate stress pattern but they have divergent secondary stress patterns.' (31) p.68: 'Primary stress falls on the final syllable if it is a long vowel, a monosyllabic root, or affixed by the perfective morpheme; otherwise it falls on the penultimate syllable.' new_statements.reading: The only long first-hand study of Stoney stress (Alexis dialect fieldwork 1994-97, plus Shaw's Morley data reviewed form by form). Right-edge system: verbs penultimate in both dialects; Alexis nouns final; final primary in Alexis when the final has a long vowel, is a monosyllabic root, or carries the perfective (lexically stressed); all long vowels stressed; secondary stress alternating right-to-left (Alexis) vs second-syllable relic of the Dakota rule (Morley, per Shaw). It keeps the catalog's right-edge, weight-hedged coding but changes what 'weight' means: RE argues Shaw's superheavy-VCC final (perfective -n + declarative) is not a syllable-weight effect at all (the [n] is a transitional nasal, final clusters are un-Stoney) but lexical stress on the perfective, while in Alexis the weight-like factor is vowel length (an Alexis innovation, not in Morley per RE pp.13-14). Morley also has imperative-final stress; Shaw says nothing about Morley nouns.

audit.recode_to: Keep kind = weight-hedged, edge = right; but re-read with Rhyasen Erdman 1997 (held) and revise the sub-fields: 'heavy' should not rest solely on Hayes n.19's 'final CVCC vs CVC, no phonemic vowel length' — RE documents underlying and derived long vowels that obligatorily attract stress (final long vowel takes primary; (22) p.64, (31) p.68) and disputes the CVCC 'superheavy' analysis (perfective morpheme lexically stressed, pp.70-71); wcls should move off 'onset-or-other' toward vowel-length (Alexis) with the coda-cluster criterion flagged as Shaw-only/disputed; prule should add the noun (final) vs verb (penult) split and the lexical triggers; srule should replace 'None described / StressTyp2 Absent' with RE's right-to-left alternating secondary stress (Alexis) vs Shaw's second-syllable secondary (Morley). Note dialect: Shaw and Wesley & Telfer = Morley (southern), RE = Alexis (northern, Isga).
audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three carried quotations verified verbatim in held files (StressTyp2 dump passage 859; Hayes 1995 p.267 (d) + n.19 RapidILL scan text; Wesley & Telfer 2022 p.3 n.3). Deciding source is a solid 1985 phonology article by the Dakota specialist, but our reading of its weight criterion comes from a one-footnote summary in Hayes 1995, and the record's own examples check already fails (10/20 Wesley & Telfer nouns).
